pr_title: Configure index sorting through index settings for logsdb
pr_body:
Indexes configured with logsdb mode currently use sorting on `[host.name, @timestamp]` by default, with keyword `host.name` getting injected if not present. This can lead to problems, if e.g. `host` is a leaf field, while sorting on an empty `host.name` is wasteful.

To fix this, the logsdb index settings provider is extended to detect when field `host.name` is present and trigger sorting on it (in addition to `@timestamp`) by injecting an index setting that is later used in `IndexSortConfig` during `IndexSettings` initialization. Otherwise, logsdb indexes are only sorted on `@timestamp` by default.

The downside is that the provider may need to inspect mappings through `MapperService` more often, a costly operation. The impact will be monitored in nightlies, once this is submitted, and logic will be further optimized as needed.

Fixes #118686

issue_context.title: LogsDB `host.name` mapping conflicts
issue_context.body:
### Description

In Elasticsearch, when using LogsDB, data streams are automatically sorted by `host.name` and `@timestamp`. To enable index sorting by default in LogsDB and avoid issues, Elasticsearch injects a default mapping for the `host.name` field as a `keyword`. However, this can cause compatibility issues when customers upgrade to LogsDB if the existing mappings for `host.name` are defined in a way that is incompatible with the default `keyword` type expected by LogsDB. Moreover, adoption of LogsDB might happen automatically for data streams matching the `logs-*-*` pattern with customers being unaware of the possible mapping conflicts.

Specifically, users who already have mappings for `host.name` with non-keyword types may encounter errors during the mapping update and/or template composition process. This happens for users using custom mappings that are not compliant with ECS. Such errors arise because Elasticsearch cannot merge incompatible field types. As a result, switching to LogsDB during an upgrade might result in mapping rejection issues, preventing a smooth transition to the new index mode for logs.

Possible solutions include:

1. **Do not inject the `host.name` field** and sort only by `@timestamp` (which already exists as a date field in data streams). This would avoid the conflict, but could result in suboptimal index sorting, affecting query performance and compression efficiency.
2. **Skip the use of `logsdb` index mode** if a conflicting mapping is detected during index creation. This would prevent logs from benefiting from the optimisations offered by LogsDB.
3. Make the `host.name` field a field that we **sort on as an "optional" sort field** (only if it does not cause mapping issues). Similarly to the first option this might result in possible suboptimal index sorting.

It is worth noting that in all cases the solution applies, anyway, on a per-data-stream basis, not affecting data streams with compatible mappings. As a result, the issue is confined to the subset of logs data streams including the incompatible `host.name` mapping only.

The second option, anyway, offers the advantage of allowing the user to adopt LogsDB at a later moment after fixing their mapping without disrupting the upgrade process and without preventing data stream rollover. It requires, anyway, a mechanism to make users aware of the issue so that they can act accordingly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that LogsDB adoption requires a rollover operation, which might result in the mapping issue surfacing days, weeks or even months after upgrading, depending on the data stream specific rollover policy.
comments:
> Do not inject the host.name field and sort only by @timestamp (which already exists as a date field in data streams). This would avoid the conflict, but could result in suboptimal index sorting, affecting query performance and compression efficiency.

I'd argue it doesn't have an effect on the efficiency of the index sorting. For example, if the data stream has a `host` field which conflicts with `host.name`, it doesn't matter whether we inject and sort by `host.name`, as that field would always be empty.

> Make the host.name field a field that we sort on as an "optional" sort field 

Sounds like that option has potential synergy with this issue: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/110792. Depending on how we implement this, it could allow us to even sort by unmapped fields.

In the short term, we prefer to skip injecting the `host.name` field and sort by `@timestamp` field only.

In the long term, it may make sense to add a _sorting_id_ field and sort by it, along with `@timestamp`. That should simplify using multiple fields, paths with wildcards or even the contents of pass-through objects, in line with how the `_tsid` uses dimension values for metrics.

Sounds like a good plan.

> In the short term, we prefer to skip injecting the host.name field and sort by @timestamp field only.

Would that be feasible for 9.0? That would make the upgrade considerably less risky and breaking.

> Would that be feasible for 9.0? That would make the upgrade considerably less risky and breaking.

That's the goal, yes.

I think we should add `Property.ServerlessPublic` also here?

Iiuc `Property.ServerlessPublic` is used to allow users to set this. This setting should *never* be set by users, it's only introduced to have the logsdb settings provider control the sort config. Do I understand this correctly?
Maybe in that case we should add `Property.PrivateIndex`? I think this would ensure that only we can use it here.
I think this validation isn't tested in `LogsIndexModeTests`? Let's add unit tests for this?

Just to verify my understanding of why we need this setting. Is it for cases where the mapping does contain a `host.name` field but the user doesn't want it to be used for sorting purposes? I suppose that is to have parity with the previous behavior where you could disable sorting by `host.name` by manually specifying just `@timestamp` as a sort field. Did I get that right?

Nit: there's a discrepancy in the naming (`SORT_ON_HOST_NAME` vs `use_default_sort_config`). The latter seems a bit more generic in case we add more fields to the default sort config. But either way, I think it makes sense to keep the name of the config option and the constant aligned.

The idea here is that, if we detect that the mappings contain a field (not object) `host.name`, it's used for sorting. Otherwise, we only sort on `@timestamp`. The rationale is that there's no point to inject `host.name` and sort on it if the mappings don't indicate that it's already present and used.

Good catch about the discrepancy - initially I had 2 settings to separately control injecting `host.name` and sorting on it. It feels cleaner to skip injection, but I'm really interested on your take here.

As mentioned in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/118968#discussion_r1899523137, I think it's important to still support dynamically mapped `host.name` fields. This could either be achieved by injecting `host.name` or by introducing this sorting hash we talked about.
Wouldn't `host.name` get injected from a dynamic template in this case? What if `host` gets dynamically mapped to a keyword as well, without `subobjects:false`?

> Wouldn't host.name get injected from a dynamic template in this case?

Not entirely sure what you mean. But there doesn't need to be a dynamic template that's specific to `host.name`, it could just be one that maps strings to keywords by default.

> What if host gets dynamically mapped to a keyword as well, without subobjects:false?

That would be an issue indeed. Still better than the current default that always injects the host.name. I suppose we'll eventually need a solution that doesn't depend on injecting a mapping but also fully supports dynamic mappings. The only solution that comes to my mind that reconciles the two is the sorting hash approach.
ok I've restored the second setting for injecting `host.name` when possible.
